title: backpressure-signals-and-tenant-throttles-draft
body:
Overview:
This is a working draft proposing a compact, experiment-friendly design for backpressure signaling and per-tenant throttles in the serving runtime. Focus is practical: low implementation surface, observable signals, and safe gradual rollouts. The aim is to reduce tail latency and catastrophic overload while preserving useful throughput for high-priority tenants.

Goals (what success looks like):
- Prevent node-level overloads that amplify latency tail (avoid head-of-line locking).
- Maintain proportional fairness across tenants with configurable weights.
- Allow short, transparent failures for low-priority traffic rather than destabilizing all workloads.
- Keep KV cache beneficial to latency-sensitive tenants and gracefully evict cold entries under pressure.
- Simple knobs for SRE/product to set global watermarks and per-tenant budgets.

Key ideas in one sentence:
Combine lightweight, latency-aware signals (queue occupancy, recent token generation time, CPU/GPU utilization) with per-tenant token-bucket admission and priority lanes; use short, adaptive timeouts plus explicit circuit-tripping for prolonged overloads; bias KV cache eviction and batch scheduling to favor in-budget/high-priority tenants.

Signal taxonomy (what we will measure and why):
- queue_len (per-lane, per-tenant): instant queue depth. Cheap and immediate signal for soft admission.
- ho_latency_est (head-of-line estimated remaining time): estimated remaining service time of the oldest queued request in a lane. Helps detect long-sync requests.
- recent_token_time_p50/p95: per-worker rolling estimate of time to generate 1 token (or per-request avg). Correlates with model/sequence length and kernel behavior.
- gpu_busy_fraction / cpu_busy_fraction: resource utilization to protect against noisy neighbors.
- kv_hit_rate_by_tenant: used to decide eviction priority and admission tradeoffs.
- retry_count_rate: rate of retries as proxy for brittle client policies (used for adaptive backoff).

Admission control components (composable):
1) Per-tenant token bucket (baseline):
   - Each tenant has a small refill rate and burst capacity configured by plan.
   - Request consumes tokens proportional to expected cost (rough proxy: expected tokens generated, or fixed cost tiers).
   - If bucket empty -> immediate 429 or queued to a short overflow lane (configurable).
   - Rationale: predictable long-term fairness and easy billing linkage.

2) Short overflow lane (soft queue):
   - Small per-node queue used for transient spikes when token bucket is empty.
   - Items in overflow lane have short deadline (e.g., 100-500ms). If deadline expires -> fail fast and emit metrics.
   - Admission into overflow lane uses a per-tenant weight to avoid head-of-line blocking.

3) Global watermarks + congestion multiplier:
   - Each worker exposes queue_len and ho_latency_est. When global queue len crosses high watermark, apply a congestion multiplier to per-tenant requests: reduce effective token refill by multiplier (e.g., 0.7 -> 70% of nominal).
   - Watermarks tuned per instance size (gpus/instance-type).

4) Priority lanes & weighted scheduling:
   - Lanes: high-priority (control plane, SLA customers), normal, best-effort.
   - Scheduler uses weighted deficit round-robin across tenants within a lane. Weights derived from plan + recent usage.

5) Timeout heuristics and hedging rules:
   - Default end-to-end timeout equals compute SLO + queue headroom.
   - For requests in overflow lane, enforce aggressive per-call timeout (shorter than normal) to reduce clogging.
   - Hedging: only for high-priority lane and when ho_latency_est exceeds threshold. Hedged request spawned to cold replica (if available) with a small delay.

KV cache interactions and eviction policy:
- Annotate KV entries with tenant and hotness score (frequency + recency).
- Under memory pressure, evict best-effort tenant entries first. High-priority tenants have retention windows.
- Admission controller will prefer admitting requests that have positive KV hit probability (est based on recent hits) to maximize throughput while under pressure.
- Cache warming for new model variants must be rate-limited to avoid blowout during rollouts.

Scheduling-level integration notes (where to plug):
- Admission checks happen at the API front layer before request enqueuing. Fast-path: per-tenant token check.
- Overflow lane and lane assignment in the node-local scheduler. Token refill can be centralized per-region or approximated locally with periodic reconciliation.
- Scheduler should expose per-tenant metrics and decisions to tracing so root-cause of throttles is visible in Console.

Graceful degradation strategies (in overload):
- Step 1: reject best-effort lane.
- Step 2: shrink per-tenant burst allowances globally using congestion multiplier.
- Step 3: deny low-priority tenants to preserve capacity for high-priority ones.
- Step 4: if tail latency remains high, selectively fall back to smaller model variant for low-priority traffic (fallthrough routing).

Observability (must-haves):
- Per-tenant: admitted_requests, rejected_requests, queue_wait_time_p50/p95, kv_hit_rate, tokens_consumed.
- Per-node: queue_len_by_lane, ho_latency_est, recent_token_time_p95, cpu/gpu_util.
- Alarms: spike in rejected_requests, sustained high queue_len, sudden drop in kv_hit_rate.

Experiment plan (MVP -> production):
MVP (2 weeks):
- Implement local per-tenant token buckets + immediate 429 on empty bucket. Expose metrics.
- Add short overflow lane with per-request deadline (no priority lanes).
Small experiment (4 weeks):
- Add global watermark detection and congestion multiplier. Tune on a staging cluster under synthetic load.
- Run A/B for 10% of nodes with overflow lane enabled for a mix of tenants.
Prod rollout (8-12 weeks):
- Add priority lanes, weighted scheduling, and KV eviction prioritization. Gradual ramp, observe Console metrics.

Metric targets (example):
- Reduce P99 tail latency by 30% under synthetic mixed workloads.
- Keep total rejected_requests < 0.2% for paid tenants at steady state.

Open questions / tradeoffs:
- Token cost estimation: use per-request size hint vs. model-estimated cost. Hint simpler but gamable; estimate harder but fairer.
- Centralized vs local token accounting: central gives strict fairness but increases control-plane load. Local approximations easier to implement and sufficient for first pass.
- Failure modes: how to prevent thundering herd when buckets refill simultaneously? Consider jittered refill or leaky bucket smoothing.

Implementation TODOs:
- [ ] Wire per-tenant token metadata into account service and local node cache.
- [ ] Add overflow lane to node scheduler with short deadlines and eviction on expiry.
- [ ] Add telemetry events for admission decisions and token consumption.
- [ ] Experiment harness to replay traffic patterns and verify fairness.

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally conservative: most of the complexity lives in the admission heuristics rather than heavy-weight global coordination. Prefer local approximations first to unblock product experiments.
- Comments, alternative heuristics, and experienced pain points (esp. around batching + kv eviction) very welcome.

References and links:
- See JIRA SR-3421 for related incident notes.
- Early proto in GITHUB:infra/queue-manager#456.
- Confluence: SR-QU-124 contains historical queue experiments and data used to pick watermarks.

Acknowledgements: initial idea sketched with Ravi and Lina during on-call rotation.
